title: Weak Ties and How Information Crosses Social Groups
text:
Suppose you were looking for a new job. Common sense says to ask those closest to you: family, close friends, the colleagues you see every day. Research on social networks suggests that this is not where most opportunities come from, and the reason is worth following.

Mark Granovetter interviewed professional and technical workers who had recently changed jobs and asked how they had heard of the position. Most had heard through a personal contact rather than an advertisement, which was not surprising. What was surprising was that the contact was usually someone they saw rarely, an old classmate or a former colleague, rather than a close friend. He called this the strength of weak ties. The mechanism is structural rather than psychological. Your close contacts tend to know one another and move in the same circles, so information reaching them has usually reached you already. A weak tie is more likely to sit in a different cluster, and therefore to carry news you could not otherwise obtain. Weak ties are the bridges between separate groups. The implication reaches beyond hiring. Ideas, rumours and innovations spread across a society along these sparse connections, so where a person sits in a network can matter as much as whom they know.
points: The starting puzzle is where job opportunities actually come from, against the assumption that close contacts matter most.
Granovetter asked recent job changers how they heard of the position, and most heard through a personal contact.
The contact was usually someone seen rarely, such as an old classmate, not a close friend.
He called this the strength of weak ties.
The reason is structural: close contacts share your circle and your information, while weak ties bridge to other clusters.
The same mechanism spreads ideas and innovations, so network position can matter as much as close relationships.
